title: Volunteer Comet Hunter Flags Potential Sun-Grazing Comet in NOAA Space Weather Satellite Data
excerpt: CCOR2 sungrazer comet report filed: Citizen scientist Mikolaj Kaszczyk has flagged a potential sun-grazing comet in NOAA’s SOLAR-1 satellite data, the most capable solar coronagraph at the Sun-Earth Lagrange point, as the NRL SunGrazer Project adapts its decades-long citizen science tradition to
content:
A volunteer comet hunter using NOAA's new CCOR2 coronagraph has flagged a potential Kreutz-family sungrazer in imagery from SOLAR-1, NOAA's first dedicated space weather satellite at the Sun-Earth Lagrange point — the latest sign that a citizen science tradition built over 30 years on aging SOHO hardware is now finding its footing on a modern successor instrument.

Mikolaj Kaszczyk filed report mk20261112050014 this morning through the Naval Research Laboratory's SunGrazer Project, flagging the candidate in three CCOR2 frames captured between 07:45 and 08:15 UTC. The object appears in the upper-left quadrant of the coronagraph's wide field of view and displays the drift pattern consistent with Kreutz family membership — the most common type of comet discovered by solar citizen scientists. The report is live on the SunGrazer platform now, awaiting independent review by NRL staff and other volunteers.

A New Eye at the Sun-Earth Boundary

CCOR2 — the Compact Coronagraph-2 — rides aboard SOLAR-1 (formerly SWFO-L1), which NOAA launched on September 24, 2025, and parked at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers (approximately 932,000 miles) from Earth, on January 23, 2026. L1 is a gravitational balance point where a satellite can maintain a fixed position on the Sun-Earth line, giving CCOR2 an unobstructed, 24-hour-a-day view of the solar corona without competing obligations to Earth observation.

That continuous coverage is what distinguishes CCOR2 from its sibling. CCOR1, which flies aboard NOAA's GOES-19 satellite in geostationary orbit, experiences daily eclipses — brief but regular periods when Earth's bulk blocks its sightline — that create gaps in the comet-detection record. CCOR2 at L1 has no such interruptions: every 15 minutes, its 2,048×1,920-pixel Active Pixel Sensor captures fresh white-light images of the corona spanning 3.5 to 26 solar radii from the Sun's center.

Crucially, CCOR2 uses a single external occulter — a disk mounted outside the optical path — to create an artificial eclipse. Unlike older designs that paired external and internal occulters, the external-only approach reduces scattered light within the optical system itself, making faint objects like dwarf Kreutz sungrazers easier to detect against the bright corona's background gradient. The 2,048×1,920 Active Pixel Sensor is the same modern detector used by Parker Solar Probe's WISPR instrument and Solar Orbiter's SoloHI, bringing CCOR2 into the same hardware generation as the most capable solar imagers currently operating in deep space.

What Is a Kreutz Sungrazer?

Kreutz sungrazers are a family of comets whose highly elliptical orbits plunge them through the Sun's outer atmosphere at perihelion — the closest point in their orbit — often within 0.01 astronomical units of the solar surface. That proximity means most dwarf members, measuring just tens of meters across, never survive: they evaporate entirely in the corona's million-degree plasma. Only the giants endure. The Great Comets of 1843 and 1882, Comet Ikeya-Seki in 1965, and Lovejoy's spectacular C/2011 W3 all passed through perihelion and lived to be seen with the naked eye.

The Kreutz family is thought to be fragments of a much larger progenitor — most likely the comet X/1106 C1, observed by Chinese and European astronomers in the 12th century, which is believed to have split during a close perihelion pass, sending its pieces on staggered orbits that continue arriving centuries later. 83 percent of SOHO's comets are Kreutz family members — a statistical dominance that reflects both how many fragments the original breakup produced and how effectively their orbital geometry funnels them through the coronagraph's narrow field of view.

Thirty Years of Citizen Science, Now Entering a New Phase

The NRL SunGrazer Project, funded by NASA and operated at the Naval Research Laboratory under principal investigator Karl Battams, Ph.D., has relied on volunteers to spot these fleeting objects since the program was formalized in the early 2000s. The scale of what amateurs have produced is extraordinary. In March 2024, the program logged its 5,000th comet discovery — a milestone reached by Hanjie Tan, a doctoral student in Prague, working in SOHO/LASCO imagery. The total now stands at more than 5,200 and continues to climb.

"The amount of data and science returned has just been beyond our wildest dreams," Battams said of the program.

SOHO, which has been operating at L1 for more than three decades — it launched December 2, 1995 — remains in service, but its LASCO coronagraph is showing its age. The transition to CCOR data has required volunteers to relearn the new instrument's field geometry and calibration. In a mid-2025 confirmations post, Battams noted that 23 comet observations over six weeks spanning June and early July had already approached the monthly discovery pace that LASCO's volunteer network had long maintained.

Looking ahead, a "Sungrazer 2.0" project — designed to extend the program's infrastructure to CCOR2 and future solar instruments — was selected for NASA seed funding in 2026, developed in partnership with the ARISA Lab. The project aims to modernize the platform that volunteers use to submit and review reports, ensuring the transition from the SOHO era does not cost the program the institutional momentum it has accumulated over three decades.

What Happens Next to Kaszczyk's Candidate

Under SunGrazer protocols, a report like Kaszczyk's — identifying a moving point-source of light in the upper-left quadrant of three consecutive CCOR2 frames — now awaits independent review and endorsement by NRL staff. Orbital geometry is the key diagnostic: Kreutz family membership is confirmed when an object's trajectory matches the family's distinctive high-inclination orbit (approximately 139 to 144 degrees) that carries it inside the Sun's corona at perihelion.

If confirmed, the comet would receive a provisional designation in the CCOR2 comet series and be forwarded to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center for formal naming. For now, Kaszczyk's report remains a "potential" — but it is publicly visible on sungrazer.nrl.navy.mil for other volunteers to independently review and endorse.

How to Participate

The SunGrazer Project is open to anyone with internet access and patience. Volunteers access real-time CCOR2 Level 3 JPEG imagery through the Space Weather Prediction Center's data portal — updated every 15 minutes around the clock — and submit reports through the NRL platform. No telescope is required, no prior astronomy background is assumed, and how-to guidance is available for new participants on the SunGrazer site.

The images are free, the data stream never sleeps, and the next comet in the catalog is waiting to be found.
